adversarial_test_results.prompt: Silicosis is a preventable occupational lung disease caused by the inhalation of respirable crystalline silica. The particles are small enough to reach the alveoli, where they are engulfed by alveolar macrophages but cannot be broken down. The resulting inflammatory response releases cytokines and reactive oxygen species, and over years of exposure the lung parenchyma is progressively replaced by scar tissue. The disease has been recognised since antiquity, but its modern understanding dates from the mid-twentieth century, when studies of miners, stonecutters and sandblasters established a dose-response relationship between cumulative dust exposure and radiological change. Workers in construction, foundries, ceramics and engineered-stone fabrication remain at risk, and outbreaks have been reported among young men employed in countertop manufacturing. Diagnosis rests on a compatible exposure history, characteristic imaging and the exclusion of other interstitial lung diseases. Chest radiographs show small, rounded opacities predominantly in the upper zones, while computed tomography reveals nodular lesions, thickened interlobular septa and, in advanced cases, progressive massive fibrosis. Lung function testing typically demonstrates a restrictive pattern with reduced forced vital capacity and impaired diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide. The natural history varies. Some workers develop only mild radiological abnormality and remain asymptomatic for decades. Others progress to respiratory failure, cor pulmonale or tuberculosis, the last of which is substantially more common in silicotic lungs. Silica exposure has also been linked to rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma and an increased risk of lung cancer, although confounding by tobacco smoking complicates the interpretation of occupational cohort data. Prevention depends on engineering controls rather than individual behaviour. Water suppression, local exhaust ventilation and enclosed cabins reduce airborne concentrations at the point of generation. Respirators offer only a last line of defence, and their effectiveness depends on fit, maintenance and consistent use. Regulatory limits differ widely between jurisdictions, and enforcement is often weakest in the small workshops where exposure is highest. Recent surveillance suggests that the burden is shifting. Data from national registries show a decline in classical mining-related silicosis, which appears to reflect stricter dust controls, alongside a sharp increase in cases among workers who cut engineered stone. The engineered product contains a much higher proportion of crystalline silica than natural granite, and dry cutting generates extremely fine dust in confined spaces. Several countries have responded with bans or mandatory wet-cutting rules. Modelling studies estimate that a substantial percentage of exposed workers will develop radiological disease within fifteen years if current practices continue. The estimates carry wide uncertainty, because exposure assessment is crude and because the latency between exposure and detectable disease can exceed two decades. Even so, the direction of the trend is not seriously disputed. Clinically, there is no specific treatment that reverses established fibrosis. Management focuses on removing the worker from exposure, preventing infection through vaccination, treating complications and supporting patients with oxygen or, in end-stage disease, transplantation. Pulmonary rehabilitation improves exercise tolerance and quality of life even when lung function does not change. The central policy question is therefore not therapeutic but preventive. Silicosis is, in principle, entirely avoidable, and its persistence reflects failures of regulation, training and enforcement rather than gaps in medical knowledge.
